claim: Perfringolysin O (PFO) is a prototypical member of a large family of pore-forming proteins.
source: Perfringolysin O (PFO) is a prototypical member of a large family of pore-forming proteins that undergo a significant reduction in height during the transition from the membrane-assembled prepore to the membrane-inserted pore.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PFO's classification within pore-forming proteins.

claim: PFO undergoes a significant reduction in height during the transition from the membrane-assembled prepore to the membrane-inserted pore.
source: Perfringolysin O (PFO) is a prototypical member of a large family of pore-forming proteins that undergo a significant reduction in height during the transition from the membrane-assembled prepore to the membrane-inserted pore.
evidence: This is supported by prior knowledge and is referenced in the manuscript with citations.

claim: Targeted application of compressive forces can catalyze the conformational change in individual PFO complexes trapped at the prepore stage.
source: Here, we show that targeted application of compressive forces can catalyze this conformational change in individual PFO complexes trapped at the prepore stage, recapitulating this critical step of the spontaneous process.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The free energy landscape determined from single molecule compression measurements is in good agreement with that obtained from molecular dynamics simulations.
source: The free energy landscape determined from these measurements is in good agreement with that obtained from molecular dynamics simulations showing that an equivalent internal force is generated by the interaction of the exposed hydrophobic residues with the membrane.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental data with computational simulations.

claim: An equivalent internal force is generated by the interaction of the exposed hydrophobic residues with the membrane.
source: The free energy landscape determined from these measurements is in good agreement with that obtained from molecular dynamics simulations showing that an equivalent internal force is generated by the interaction of the exposed hydrophobic residues with the membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from molecular dynamics simulations.

claim: The hydrophobic force is transmitted across the entire structure to produce a compressive stress across a distant, otherwise stable domain.
source: This hydrophobic force is transmitted across the entire structure to produce a compressive stress across a distant, otherwise stable domain, catalyzing its transition from an extended to compact conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental and computational data.

claim: The compressive stress catalyzes the transition of the D2 domain from an extended to compact conformation.
source: This hydrophobic force is transmitted across the entire structure to produce a compressive stress across a distant, otherwise stable domain, catalyzing its transition from an extended to compact conformation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and simulations.

claim: Single molecule compression is likely to become an important tool to investigate conformational transitions in membrane proteins.
source: Single molecule compression is likely to become an important tool to investigate conformational transitions in membrane proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications of the technique.

claim: Single macromolecules can be mechanically stretched with exact knowledge of the associated forces.
source: The initial demonstration that single macromolecules could be mechanically stretched with exact knowledge of the associated forces (Smith et al., 1992; Kellermayer et al., 1997; Rief et al., 1997; Tskhovrebova et al., 1997) has enabled unprecedented access to measurements of the physical and chemical inter-molecular interactions (Bippes and Muller, 2011; Bustamante et al., 2000; Fisher et al., 2000; Hu and Li, 2014; Zhuang and Rief, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Pulling on single molecules with tensile forces has enabled detailed probing of functional and structural transitions within proteins.
source: Moreover, pulling on single molecules with tensile forces has enabled detailed probing of functional and structural transitions within proteins, in particular those that involve a separation of specific structural elements (Puchner and Gaub, 2012; Zhang et al., 2009; del Rio et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Tensile forces cannot be used to probe transitions that involve a decrease in the distance between structural elements.
source: Yet, tensile forces cannot be used to probe transitions that involve a decrease in the distance between structural elements such as the closing of a substrate access gate, for example, as the force acts in a direction opposite to the structural movement.
evidence: This is based on logical inference from the nature of tensile forces.

claim: PFO undergoes a significant reduction in the distance between the D1 and D4 domains during pore formation.
source: Perfringolysin O (PFO) is an intriguing pore-forming toxin that undergoes a significant reduction in the distance between two of its domains during pore formation (Gilbert, 2005; Hotze and Tweten, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During the prepore-to-pore transition, the distance between the D1 and D4 domains is reduced as a result of conformational changes in the D2 domain.
source: During the prepore-to-pore transition, the distance between the D1 and D4 domains is reduced as a result of conformational changes in the D2 domain (Figure 1): this domain is elongated in the prepore but collapses into a more compact structure in the pore, largely accounting for the remarkable 40 Å decrease in height relative to the bilayer surface first observed by atomic force microscopy (AFM) (Czajkowsky et al., 2004; Tilley et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The D2 domain is elongated in the prepore but collapses into a more compact structure in the pore.
source: During the prepore-to-pore transition, the distance between the D1 and D4 domains is reduced as a result of conformational changes in the D2 domain (Figure 1): this domain is elongated in the prepore but collapses into a more compact structure in the pore, largely accounting for the remarkable 40 Å decrease in height relative to the bilayer surface first observed by atomic force microscopy (AFM) (Czajkowsky et al., 2004; Tilley et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1.

claim: The D2 domain collapse largely accounts for the remarkable 40 Å decrease in height relative to the bilayer surface.
source: During the prepore-to-pore transition, the distance between the D1 and D4 domains is reduced as a result of conformational changes in the D2 domain (Figure 1): this domain is elongated in the prepore but collapses into a more compact structure in the pore, largely accounting for the remarkable 40 Å decrease in height relative to the bilayer surface first observed by atomic force microscopy (AFM) (Czajkowsky et al., 2004; Tilley et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1.

claim: An α-helical bundle (the Trans-Membrane Helices) in the D3 domain converts into an amphipathic β-sheet that inserts in the bilayer and lines the aqueous membrane pore during the prepore-to-pore transition.
source: Also within this prepore-to-pore step, an α-helical bundle (the Trans-Membrane Helices (TMHs)) in the D3 domain converts into an amphipathic β-sheet that inserts in the bilayer and lines the aqueous membrane pore.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the structural changes in PFO.

claim: The mechanism by which changes in the D2 and D3 domains are coordinated remains unresolved.
source: While these changes in the D2 and D3 domains have been firmly established, the mechanism by which these changes are coordinated remains unresolved.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The physical processes associated with long-distance structural communication in proteins are poorly understood in general.
source: In fact, the physical processes associated with long-distance structural communication in proteins are poorly understood in general (Cui and Karplus, 2008; Whitley and Lee, 2009; Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Intra-protein stresses are the driving force of the structural coordination between the D2 and D3 domains.
source: Herein, using single molecule compressive force spectroscopy and single molecule AFM together with all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we demonstrate that intra-protein stresses are the driving force of the structural coordination between the D2 and D3 domains and, ultimately, the catalyst of the collapse of the D2 domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and simulations.

claim: Intra-protein stresses are the catalyst of the collapse of the D2 domain.
source: Herein, using single molecule compressive force spectroscopy and single molecule AFM together with all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we demonstrate that intra-protein stresses are the driving force of the structural coordination between the D2 and D3 domains and, ultimately, the catalyst of the collapse of the D2 domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and simulations.

claim: The D2 and TMHs directly contact each other in the PFO prepore.
source: As the D2 and TMHs directly contact each other in the PFO prepore and are well separated in the pore, it was previously suggested that the loss of these contacts during the prepore-to-pore transition might have precipitated the collapse of an inherently unstable D2 domain (Czajkowsky et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: The D2 and TMHs are well separated in the pore.
source: As the D2 and TMHs directly contact each other in the PFO prepore and are well separated in the pore, it was previously suggested that the loss of these contacts during the prepore-to-pore transition might have precipitated the collapse of an inherently unstable D2 domain (Czajkowsky et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: It was previously suggested that the loss of D2-TMH contacts during the prepore-to-pore transition might have precipitated the collapse of an inherently unstable D2 domain.
source: As the D2 and TMHs directly contact each other in the PFO prepore and are well separated in the pore, it was previously suggested that the loss of these contacts during the prepore-to-pore transition might have precipitated the collapse of an inherently unstable D2 domain (Czajkowsky et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a prior hypothesis cited from previous work.

claim: Extensive equilibrium MD simulations (>0.3 µs) of a PFO monomer without the TMHs shows that the D2 domain remains in an extended conformation in the absence of the TMHs interactions.
source: However, extensive equilibrium MD simulations (>0.3 µs) of a PFO monomer without the TMHs shows that the D2 domain remains in an extended conformation in the absence of the TMHs interactions, fluctuating in height by only a few Å (2.9 Å RMS height deviation) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The D2 domain fluctuates in height by only a few Å (2.9 Å RMS height deviation) in the absence of TMHs interactions.
source: However, extensive equilibrium MD simulations (>0.3 µs) of a PFO monomer without the TMHs shows that the D2 domain remains in an extended conformation in the absence of the TMHs interactions, fluctuating in height by only a few Å (2.9 Å RMS height deviation) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by MD simulation data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The loss of contact with the TMHs alone is insufficient to trigger the conversion of the D2 domain into a compact structure.
source: Thus, the loss of contact with the TMHs alone is insufficient to trigger the conversion of the D2 domain into a compact structure, a conclusion consistent with recent work showing that the TMHs in the thermally trapped PFO prepore are unfolded with significant conformational freedom (Sato et al., 2013) while cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) images of a related cytotoxin, pneumolysin, showed that the D2 domain in this state is in its extended conformation (Tilley et al., 2005).
evidence: This is inferred from MD simulation data and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The TMHs in the thermally trapped PFO prepore are unfolded with significant conformational freedom.
source: Thus, the loss of contact with the TMHs alone is insufficient to trigger the conversion of the D2 domain into a compact structure, a conclusion consistent with recent work showing that the TMHs in the thermally trapped PFO prepore are unfolded with significant conformational freedom (Sato et al., 2013) while cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) images of a related cytotoxin, pneumolysin, showed that the D2 domain in this state is in its extended conformation (Tilley et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Cryo-EM images of pneumolysin showed that the D2 domain in the thermally trapped prepore state is in its extended conformation.
source: Thus, the loss of contact with the TMHs alone is insufficient to trigger the conversion of the D2 domain into a compact structure, a conclusion consistent with recent work showing that the TMHs in the thermally trapped PFO prepore are unfolded with significant conformational freedom (Sato et al., 2013) while cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) images of a related cytotoxin, pneumolysin, showed that the D2 domain in this state is in its extended conformation (Tilley et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Fully extended TMHs are of a sufficient length to contact the bilayer surface.
source: Closer inspection of this prepore conformation, in fact, reveals that fully extended TMHs are of a sufficient length to contact the bilayer surface (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The extended conformation of TMHs exposes hydrophobic residues to water.
source: This extended conformation exposes hydrophobic residues in the TMHs to water, and so the membrane contact would generate a bilayer-directed hydrophobic force on the TMHs, driving them toward the membrane interior.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis.

claim: Membrane contact generates a bilayer-directed hydrophobic force on the TMHs, driving them toward the membrane interior.
source: This extended conformation exposes hydrophobic residues in the TMHs to water, and so the membrane contact would generate a bilayer-directed hydrophobic force on the TMHs, driving them toward the membrane interior.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis and knowledge of hydrophobic interactions.

claim: A hydrophobic force exerted on a water-exposed transmembrane region has been reported in the folding of bacteriorhodopsin.
source: Such a hydrophobic force exerted on a water-exposed transmembrane region has been reported in the folding of bacteriorhodopsin (Kessler et al., 2006) and implicated in the translocon-mediated membrane integration of transmembrane helices (Ismail et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Hydrophobic force has been implicated in the translocon-mediated membrane integration of transmembrane helices.
source: Such a hydrophobic force exerted on a water-exposed transmembrane region has been reported in the folding of bacteriorhodopsin (Kessler et al., 2006) and implicated in the translocon-mediated membrane integration of transmembrane helices (Ismail et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Steered MD simulations with a downward constant force on the TMHs reveal that the most significant structural effect is the collapse of the D2 domain.
source: To examine the effect of this bilayer-directed force on the conformation of the protein, we employed steered MD simulations, applying a downward constant force specifically on the TMHs. These calculations reveal that the most significant structural effect of this force is the collapse of the D2 domain (Figure 2B), with the rest of the structure remaining largely unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by steered MD simulation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The rest of the PFO structure remains largely unchanged during the D2 domain collapse in steered MD simulations.
source: To examine the effect of this bilayer-directed force on the conformation of the protein, we employed steered MD simulations, applying a downward constant force specifically on the TMHs. These calculations reveal that the most significant structural effect of this force is the collapse of the D2 domain (Figure 2B), with the rest of the structure remaining largely unchanged (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by steered MD simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The tensile force on the TMHs is effectively transmitted through the protein to generate a compressive stress across the D2 domain that can catalyze its collapse.
source: That is, the tensile force on the TMHs is effectively transmitted through the protein to generate a compressive stress across the D2 domain that can catalyze its collapse.
evidence: This is inferred from the steered MD simulation results.

claim: During the simulations, after modest initial changes in conformation, the protein structure remained relatively stable owing to the presence of an energy barrier that prevented further conformational changes.
source: During the simulations, after modest initial changes in conformation, the protein structure remained relatively stable owing to the presence of an energy barrier that prevented further conformational changes.
evidence: This is observed in the steered MD simulations.

claim: The energy barrier was overcome, and the height dropped rapidly to a value ∼40 Å lower than its initial height.
source: Finally, this barrier was overcome, and the height dropped rapidly to a value ∼40 Å lower than its initial height (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is observed in the steered MD simulations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the final conformation, the lower portion of the D2 domain is still a β-sheet and lies almost perpendicular on the surface of the D4 domain, pivoting at Lys381.
source: In this final conformation, the lower portion of the D2 domain is still a β-sheet and lies almost perpendicular on the surface of the D4 domain, pivoting at Lys381.
evidence: This is observed in the steered MD simulations.

claim: The D2 domain remains in the compact conformation even after the force is relieved (for >40 ns).
source: More importantly, the D2 domain remains in this compact conformation even after the force is relieved (for >40 ns) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting that this conformation is a relatively stable state.
evidence: This is observed in MD simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The compact conformation of the D2 domain is a relatively stable state.
source: More importantly, the D2 domain remains in this compact conformation even after the force is relieved (for >40 ns) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), suggesting that this conformation is a relatively stable state.
evidence: This is inferred from the MD simulation data showing the conformation persists after force removal.

claim: The D2/D4 interface in the compact conformation covers 842 Å².
source: The D2/D4 interface in this conformation covers 842 Å (Kellermayer et al., 1997) similar to that observed for interfacial contacts in oligomeric proteins (Miller et al., 1987), and the buried hydrophobic residues (Phe75, Tyr389, Tyr415) in the interface (Figure 2C) likely contributed to the stability of this compact state.
evidence: This is measured from the simulation structure and compared to known values from citations.

claim: The D2/D4 interface area is similar to that observed for interfacial contacts in oligomeric proteins.
source: The D2/D4 interface in this conformation covers 842 Å (Kellermayer et al., 1997) similar to that observed for interfacial contacts in oligomeric proteins (Miller et al., 1987), and the buried hydrophobic residues (Phe75, Tyr389, Tyr415) in the interface (Figure 2C) likely contributed to the stability of this compact state.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to cited values from prior work.

claim: The buried hydrophobic residues (Phe75, Tyr389, Tyr415) in the D2/D4 interface likely contributed to the stability of the compact state.
source: The D2/D4 interface in this conformation covers 842 Å (Kellermayer et al., 1997) similar to that observed for interfacial contacts in oligomeric proteins (Miller et al., 1987), and the buried hydrophobic residues (Phe75, Tyr389, Tyr415) in the interface (Figure 2C) likely contributed to the stability of this compact state.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The hydrophobic residues Phe75, Tyr389, and Tyr415 are highly conserved in the cholesterol-dependent cytolysins (CDC) family.
source: As these residues are highly conserved in the cholesterol-dependent cytolysins (CDC) family (Supplementary file 1), it is possible that this structure is a common feature of other CDC toxins.
evidence: This is supported by data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The collapsed D2 structure may be a common feature of other CDC toxins.
source: As these residues are highly conserved in the cholesterol-dependent cytolysins (CDC) family (Supplementary file 1), it is possible that this structure is a common feature of other CDC toxins.
evidence: This is speculated based on the conservation of key residues.

claim: Different forces consistently produced similar results in steered MD simulations, but the time scale was significantly longer at lower forces.
source: For these simulations, the applied force was 250 pN; different forces consistently produced similar results, but the time scale was significantly longer at lower forces (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is observed in steered MD simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The collapsed structure is consistent with the electron-density profile of the pneumolysin pore by cryo-EM.
source: Overall this collapsed structure is consistent with the electron-density profile of the pneumolysin pore by cryo-EM (Tilley et al., 2005) (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to cited cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Extensive adaptive biasing force (ABF) simulations yielded the energy landscape along the reaction coordinate, the height of the D3 domain.
source: To further understand the energy associated with this transition, extensive adaptive biasing force (ABF) simulations (Chipot and Hénin, 2005) yielded the energy landscape along the reaction coordinate, the height of the D3 domain.
evidence: This is supported by ABF simulation data.

claim: The energy landscape exhibits a broad minimum at heights associated with the prepore conformation (from −10 to 8 Å).
source: This landscape (Figure 2D) exhibits a broad minimum at heights associated with the prepore conformation (from −10 to 8 Å) and a local minimum at heights associated with the pore conformation (centered at ∼40 Å), separated by an energy barrier of ∼23 kcal/mol (∼38 kBT) from the prepore minimum.
evidence: This is shown in the ABF simulation data in Figure 2D.

claim: The energy landscape exhibits a local minimum at heights associated with the pore conformation (centered at ∼40 Å).
source: This landscape (Figure 2D) exhibits a broad minimum at heights associated with the prepore conformation (from −10 to 8 Å) and a local minimum at heights associated with the pore conformation (centered at ∼40 Å), separated by an energy barrier of ∼23 kcal/mol (∼38 kBT) from the prepore minimum.
evidence: This is shown in the ABF simulation data in Figure 2D.

claim: The prepore and pore conformations are separated by an energy barrier of ∼23 kcal/mol (∼38 kBT).
source: This landscape (Figure 2D) exhibits a broad minimum at heights associated with the prepore conformation (from −10 to 8 Å) and a local minimum at heights associated with the pore conformation (centered at ∼40 Å), separated by an energy barrier of ∼23 kcal/mol (∼38 kBT) from the prepore minimum.
evidence: This is shown in the ABF simulation data in Figure 2D.

claim: The extended structure of the D2 domain is associated with the energetically minimized conformation of PFO.
source: Thus, the extended structure of the D2 domain is indeed associated with the energetically minimized conformation of PFO.
evidence: This is inferred from the ABF simulation results showing the prepore conformation at the energy minimum.

claim: There is a sharp rise in the energy at ∼25 Å, where the energy increases by ∼17 kcal/mol over a distance of ∼6 Å.
source: Of note, there is a sharp rise in the energy at ∼25 Å, where the energy increases by ∼17 kcal/mol over a distance of ∼6 Å.
evidence: This is observed in the ABF simulation data.

claim: A barrier height of ∼17 kcal/mol would require a time frame of days to be overcome by thermal fluctuations alone.
source: Such a barrier height would require a time frame of days to be overcome by thermal fluctuations alone (see 'Materials and methods'), far longer than the observed timescales of the prepore-to-pore transition (Hotze et al., 2001).
evidence: This is calculated based on the barrier height and cited timescales.

claim: The time frame to overcome the barrier by thermal fluctuations is far longer than the observed timescales of the prepore-to-pore transition.
source: Such a barrier height would require a time frame of days to be overcome by thermal fluctuations alone (see 'Materials and methods'), far longer than the observed timescales of the prepore-to-pore transition (Hotze et al., 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of calculated and observed timescales with citation.

claim: The primary barrier that must be reduced by the force generated by the bilayer-TMHs interaction is at ∼25 Å.
source: Thus, this is the primary barrier that must be reduced by the force generated by the bilayer-TMHs interaction in order to drive PFO into its pore conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the ABF simulation data and analysis.

claim: PFOG57C-S190C spontaneously assembles into prepore complexes on the membrane like the wild-type protein.
source: In this regard, a mutant protein, PFOG57C-S190C, has been identified that spontaneously assembles into prepore complexes on the membrane like the wild-type protein but does not proceed to the pore state owing to a disulfide bridge that inhibits the restructuring of the TMHs (Figure 3A) (Czajkowsky et al., 2004; Hotze et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: PFOG57C-S190C does not proceed to the pore state owing to a disulfide bridge that inhibits the restructuring of the TMHs.
source: In this regard, a mutant protein, PFOG57C-S190C, has been identified that spontaneously assembles into prepore complexes on the membrane like the wild-type protein but does not proceed to the pore state owing to a disulfide bridge that inhibits the restructuring of the TMHs (Figure 3A) (Czajkowsky et al., 2004; Hotze et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: When the disulfide constraint is removed by adding DTT, PFOG57C-S190C quickly converts into a native-like pore.
source: When this constraint is removed by adding Dithiothreitol (DTT), this mutant quickly converts into a native-like pore (Czajkowsky et al., 2004; Hotze et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PFOG57C-S190C enables investigation of just the energy barrier of the D2 collapse under compressive forces, without any complicating effects associated with the D3-bilayer interaction.
source: Thus, this mutant enables investigation of just the energy barrier of the D2 collapse under compressive forces, without any complicating effects associated with the D3-bilayer interaction (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the properties of the mutant and shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Steered MD simulations confirmed that under compressive forces mimicking those applied with AFM, the D2 domain of PFOG57C-S190C recapitulates the same collapse as that of the D2 domain under tensile forces applied to the TMHs.
source: Steered MD simulations confirmed that under compressive forces mimicking those that would be applied with AFM, the D2 domain of this mutant recapitulates the same collapse as that of the D2 domain under tensile forces applied to the TMHs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by steered MD simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Direct application of constant compressive forces with an AFM tip to individual PFOG57C-S190C prepore complexes reproducibly induced the characteristic height reduction in the absence of any reducing agent.
source: Indeed, direct application of constant compressive forces with an AFM tip to individual PFOG57C-S190C prepore complexes reproducibly induced the characteristic height reduction in the absence of any reducing agent, leaving the general morphology of the complexes otherwise unchanged (Figure 3C and additional images are presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by AFM experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The compressive force application leaves the general morphology of the complexes otherwise unchanged.
source: Indeed, direct application of constant compressive forces with an AFM tip to individual PFOG57C-S190C prepore complexes reproducibly induced the characteristic height reduction in the absence of any reducing agent, leaving the general morphology of the complexes otherwise unchanged (Figure 3C and additional images are presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is observed in AFM experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The pore-like structure does not revert back to the prepore conformation upon removing the applied force.
source: We note that this pore-like structure does not revert back to the prepore conformation upon removing the applied force, indicating that this compact structure is relatively stable, consistent with the MD simulations.
evidence: This is observed in AFM experiments.

claim: The compact structure is relatively stable.
source: We note that this pore-like structure does not revert back to the prepore conformation upon removing the applied force, indicating that this compact structure is relatively stable, consistent with the MD simulations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the structure does not revert and is consistent with MD simulations.

claim: The applied force (110 pN/monomer) is >10-fold smaller than the force required to break a covalent bond over this time period.
source: We further note that this applied force (110 pN/monomer) is >10-fold smaller than the force required to break a covalent bond over this time period (see 'Materials and methods') (Grandbois et al., 1999).
evidence: This is calculated based on the applied force and cited values for covalent bond breaking.

claim: The force-catalyzed conversion is dependent on the magnitude and the duration of the applied force.
source: As expected for a thermally driven transition, this force-catalyzed conversion is dependent on the magnitude and the duration of the applied force (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is observed in AFM experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Each 1s and 5s dataset is well described by the same single barrier model.
source: Each 1s and 5s dataset is well described by the same single barrier model (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown by fitting the data in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Simultaneous fitting of both 1s and 5s datasets yielded xβ = 5.1 ± 0.8 Å and ∆Go = 16.3 ± 0.6 kcal/mol.
source: Thus, we simultaneously fitted both datasets to the above equations, yielding xβ = 5.1 ± 0.8 Å and ∆Go = 16.3 ± 0.6 kcal/mol (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is obtained from fitting AFM experimental data.

claim: The energy barrier from AFM experiments is smaller than that observed in previous single molecule protein domain unfolding experiments.
source: This energy barrier is smaller than that observed in previous single molecule protein domain unfolding experiments (Fernandez et al., 2010; Dietz and Rief, 2008), as might be expected since the D2 domain is not unfolded during this transition.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison to cited prior work.

claim: The D2 domain is not unfolded during the prepore-to-pore transition.
source: This energy barrier is smaller than that observed in previous single molecule protein domain unfolding experiments (Fernandez et al., 2010; Dietz and Rief, 2008), as might be expected since the D2 domain is not unfolded during this transition.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis and simulation data.

claim: There is excellent agreement between the experimental values (xβ = 5.1 ± 0.8 Å and ∆Go = 16.3 ± 0.6 kcal/mol) and the ABF calculations (6 Å and 17 kcal/mol, respectively).
source: Importantly, there is excellent agreement between the experimental values and the aforementioned ABF calculations (6 Å and 17 kcal/mol, respectively), thereby providing quantitative support for the model.
evidence: This is shown by comparison of experimental and computational results.

claim: The agreement between experimental and computational values provides quantitative support for the model.
source: Importantly, there is excellent agreement between the experimental values and the aforementioned ABF calculations (6 Å and 17 kcal/mol, respectively), thereby providing quantitative support for the model.
evidence: This is inferred from the agreement between experimental and computational results.

claim: Any weakening of the TMHs-bilayer hydrophobic interaction is expected to cause a measurable reduction in the rate of prepore-to-pore transition.
source: Since the hydrophobic force generated by the TMHs-bilayer interaction is critical for the prepore-to-pore transition, any weakening of this interaction is expected to cause a measurable reduction in the rate of transition.
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed mechanism.

claim: Detergent binding to hydrophobic residues in the TMHs should reduce the hydrophobic force on the TMHs.
source: Therefore, we investigated the prepore-to-pore transition in the presence of a detergent (n-dodecyl-β-D-maltoside, DDM), since detergent binding to hydrophobic residues in the TMHs should reduce this hydrophobic force on the TMHs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of detergent-protein interactions and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Incubating DDM with the mutant PFOG57C-S190C prepore complexes, followed by the addition of DTT, prevents conversion to the pore-like structure.
source: As shown in Figure 4B, incubating DDM with the mutant PFOG57C-S190C prepore complexes, followed by the addition of DTT, prevents conversion to the pore-like structure.
evidence: This is observed in AFM experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The inhibition effect of DDM was dependent on the concentration of detergent, with a maximal inhibition observed with nearly 20 µM DDM.
source: This effect was dependent on the concentration of detergent, with a maximal inhibition observed with nearly 20 µM DDM (Figure 4B), a similar concentration as that observed for binding to exposed hydrophobic regions in other proteins (Kragh-Hansen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is observed in AFM experimental data shown in Figure 4B and compared to cited values.

claim: The DDM concentration for maximal inhibition is similar to that observed for binding to exposed hydrophobic regions in other proteins.
source: This effect was dependent on the concentration of detergent, with a maximal inhibition observed with nearly 20 µM DDM (Figure 4B), a similar concentration as that observed for binding to exposed hydrophobic regions in other proteins (Kragh-Hansen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to cited values from prior work.

claim: Intra-protein forces may be a critical factor in driving coordinated conformational changes between distant domains in many other systems.
source: In summary, the combination of single molecule measurements and MD computations has enabled direct identification of the essential role of intra-protein forces in driving the PFO complex into its final pore conformation (Figure 4C). We speculate that such intra-protein forces may also be a critical factor in driving coordinated conformational changes between distant domains in many other systems, which are presently not fully characterized mechanistically (Cui and Karplus, 2008; Changeux and Edelstein, 2005).
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings in PFO and cited prior work.

claim: Single molecule compressive force spectroscopy can be an effective means to probe and quantify physical mechanisms of conformational coordination within membrane proteins.
source: These results also demonstrate that single molecule compressive force spectroscopy can be an effective means by which previously inaccessible physical mechanisms of conformational coordination within membrane proteins in particular may now be probed and quantified.
evidence: This is inferred from the successful application of the technique in this study.

claim: The complete PFOG57C-S190C rings contain 36 subunits.
source: Based on the radial periodicity of the monomers in the complete rings (Czajkowsky et al., 2004) and high-resolution images of the rings (data not published), the complete rings contain 36 subunits.
evidence: This is determined from structural analysis with citation and unpublished data.

claim: The total applied force range used in AFM experiments (1800 pN to 3800 pN) corresponds to 50 pN to 106 pN per monomer.
source: Thus, in the text, we referred to the applied force either with respect to the entire complex or to each monomer (dividing the total applied force by 36). As such, the total applied force range used here (1800 pN to –3800 pN) corresponds to 50 pN to –106 pN per monomer, which is at least an order of magnitude smaller than the force needed to break a covalent bond over this time frame (1400 pN to –2000 pN) (Grandbois et al., 1999).
evidence: This is calculated from the total force divided by 36 subunits.

claim: More than 30 individual measurements were performed at each applied force, resulting in more than 600 individual single molecule measurements.
source: On average, more than 30 individual measurements were performed at each applied force, resulting in more than 600 individual single molecule measurements obtained from tens of samples and using tens of different AFM cantilevers.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and sample size.

claim: Using an attempt frequency of 10^7/s yields ∆Go = 16.3 ± 0.6 kcal/mol from the AFM data.
source: Using an attempt frequency of 107/s, consistent with previous force spectroscopy studies (Yu et al., 2012), we obtain (using Equation 2): ∆Go = 16.3 ± 0.6 kcal/mol.

claim: For the barrier height obtained from ABF calculations (17 kcal/mol), the force-free lifetime is approximately 1.7 days.
source: For the barrier height obtained from the ABF calculations (17 kcal/mol), using a similar attempt frequency and Equation 2 yields ko = 6.9 × 10-6/s, which corresponds to a (force-free) lifetime of ∼1.7 days.
